Q: How to implement custom instruction files (e.g., MYTOOL.md) that LLM agents recognize A:

There isn’t a universal standard where LLMs automatically recognize MYTOOL.md the way they treat something like AGENT.md or SKILL.md. Those files feel special because specific tools (like GitHub Copilot or OpenAI Codex) have hardcoded conventions or training patterns around them.

So if you want your own MYTOOL.md to behave similarly, you have to recreate that “specialness” yourself through structure + tooling—not just the filename. What actually going on behind SKILL.md / AGENT.md These files work well

because: They follow predictable schemas The agent runtime explicitly

loads them Prompts inject them automatically Sometimes fine-tuning or

system prompts reinforce them So the "framework" you're looking for is

not a library - it's a pattern:

"Convention + Loader + Prompt Injection + Execution Loop"

How to Build Your Own MYTOOL.md System

1 Define a Strict Schema (this is critical) Don't make it free-form

markdown. Give it structure the agent can reliably parse.

Example:

# MYTOOL: CodeRefactorer

## PURPOSE

Refactor code for readability and performance.

## INPUT

- language: string

- code: string

## OUTPUT

- refactored_code: string

- explanation: string

## RULES

- Preserve functionality

- Improve naming conventions

- Reduce complexity

## EXAMPLES

### Input

language:

-javascript

-code: var x=1;

### Output

let count = 1;

Think of this like a lightweight DSL (domain-specific language), not

just docs

2. Build a Loader (this is what tools like Copilot do internally)

You need a layer that: Scans repo for \*.md (or specifically MYTOOL.md)

Parses sections Converts them into structured JSON Injects into prompts

Example (pseudo): const tool = parseMarkdown("MYTOOL.md");

const systemPrompt = You are an AI agent.

Available tools: \${JSON.stringify(tool);

3. Create a Tool Invocation Protocol LLMs won't "decide" to use your tool unless you define how. Example pattern

" When a task matches a tool: Respond with:

TOOL_CALL: name: CodeRefactorer input: language: javascript code: ... "

Then your runtime: Detects TOOL_CALL Executes logic (or calls another LLM) Feeds result back

4. Add a Planning Layer (this is what makes it feel like an "agent")

Instead of direct answering: User -> LLM -> Answer

Do : User -> LLM (Planner) -> decides tool -> executes tool -> returns result

This is how modern agent frameworks behave.

5. Optional: Register It as a "Skill".

Tools like Codex or Copilot sometimes treat skills specially because:

They are indexed

They have metadata

They are preloaded

You can simulate this by: Keeping a /skills folder Loading all .md files at startup Giving each a name, trigger, capability.

Q: Comment portion of a line in a REG file? A:

It's enough to put semicolon before comment on the same line. In another words, semicolon before comment is supported by reg file on a line with registry entry as well as a full-line of comment.

; This is a comment

References

  • Minus sign to delete, semicolon to comment and IF/ENDIF mentioned here: MSDN: Registry File (Compact 2013).

Q: angular 7 TypeError: Cannot read property 'hasOwnProperty' of undefined A:

This error topic is a bit outdated, but I've fought a lot with this angular DI issue. I've found a solution for missing dependencies that raise hasOwnProperty error (or 'ɵprov' for old angular versions).

It's related to barrel files (explanation here). Those files (named index.ts), some times are not correctly resolved (more here).

I got hit by hasOwnProperty error, when trying to understand why a route, structured according to Angular Router docs, didn't have a resolved dependency in canActivate property.

My solution was changing the import of that dependency (a service). I changed it from 'app/core' (a barrel), to a direct import to it, in 'app/core/auth/user-route-access-service'. That service was provided in root.

How to debug (tested with Angular 10 and 11)

Useful if you don't have a clue where to fix. Using Chrome, open developer tools with F12. Open the page where the error is being logged, then click in resolveNgModuleDep.

Add a logpoint a little above from where you are:

With the content 'Module: ', data._moduleType.name

Then click here:

And add another logpoint here:

With the content 'Component: ', futureARS.component.name, ' canActivate=', canActivate

Refresh page with F5

After that, you will be able to locate the component (surrounded by the module name), whose route has an invalid canActivate property, which creates the problem.
